episodes.title: Possible: Satya Nadella on making human and token capital compound
episodes.summary: In this recent episode of Possible, Reid Hoffman sits down with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella fresh off Microsoft Build 2026. The conversation goes wide: how AI is reshaping work, business, and society—and why the transformation sweeping through software development today is only a preview of what's coming for all knowledge work. Satya makes the case that human capital and "token capital" are now deeply intertwined, that companies—not just countries—must build their own AI capabilities, and that the organizations best positioned to thrive are those that can leverage their unique expertise inside intelligent systems. Reid and Satya also explore Microsoft's enterprise AI vision, Reid's work with Manas on AI-powered scientific discovery, lessons from past technological revolutions, and why demonstrating real, tangible benefits may be the most important thing the industry can do to earn—and keep—the public's trust. episodes.title: Steven Pressfield: The Hero’s Journey, Resistance, and Becoming the Artist You’re Meant to Be [From the Archive]
episodes.summary: Episode Description: This is a From the Archive episode with one of my favorite guests: Steven Pressfield. Steven Pressfield has spent his career writing about war, creativity, discipline, storytelling, and the inner battle every artist faces. In this archive conversation, James and Steven explore how stories work—and why the same structures that power novels and movies also show up in real life. They begin with The Legend of Bagger Vance , which Pressfield built from the structure of the Bhagavad Gita . James connects that idea to his own writing, where ancient texts like the Yoga Sutras became frameworks for modern essays about entrepreneurship. Their point is simple: if a story has survived thousands of years, it probably contains a structure worth studying. From there, the conversation moves into the hero’s journey. The ordinary world. The call to adventure. The refusal of the call. The mentor. The threshold. The extraordinary world. The tests, allies, enemies, ordeal, return, and gift. But Pressfield pushes the idea further. In real life, people do not always answer the call. Some people refuse it for years. Some cross the threshold and then run back. Some sacrifice security, status, money, family expectations, or even relationships to follow the deeper pull of their lives. James shares his own story of walking out of a finance job after three days, leaving his coat on the chair, taking the elevator down 40 floors, getting on a train, and never returning. Pressfield recognizes it immediately as a real-life threshold moment. The conversation then turns to The Artist’s Journey . Pressfield explains that the hero’s journey ends when the hero returns home with a gift. The artist’s journey begins when the artist asks: What is the gift I am meant to give? What is my material? What is my voice? What am I here to make? They discuss Resistance as the real villain in every story, why the question “Who am I?” often drives the inciting incident, why villains often do not change, why opening and closing images matter, and why genres have rules that writers ignore at their own risk. This episode is a masterclass in story, but it is also a meditation on identity. The deeper question is not just how to write a story. It is how to recognize the story already trying to live through you. Editorial Note: This is a "From the Archive" episode. References to “new” or “upcoming” books, projects, or events reflect the timing of the original recording. What You’ll Learn: Why Steven Pressfield built The Legend of Bagger Vance on the structure of the Bhagavad Gita . How ancient myths and spiritual texts can become frameworks for modern stories. Why the hero’s journey begins only when the hero answers the call. What separates the ordinary world from the extraordinary world. Why Resistance appears immediately after the call to action. Why crossing the threshold changes how other people see you—and how you see yourself. How the artist’s journey begins after the hero’s journey ends. Why the artist’s real question is: What gift am I bringing back? How to go deeper into theme instead of just telling a surface-level story. Why success, awards, money, and status can become forms of Resistance. How dreams, intuition, and recurring ideas can point toward a person’s real work. Why every strong story creates a first pole and second pole: the question and the answer. Why the villain may be a person, a force, or Resistance itself. Why genre conventions matter, even for experienced writers. How opening and closing images can reveal the full emotional transformation of a story.
